opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, because in quant the feedback loop is brutal but honest. You put on a strategy, and the P&L tells you whether you were right, sometimes within days. In large models the signal is much noisier and much slower. You might spend months on a direction and still not be sure whether it mattered, or whether something else in the pipeline was responsible for the improvement.

So I try to rely on a few things.

The first is first-principles reasoning about where the bottleneck actually is. If you look at the whole system, data, architecture, training efficiency, post-training, inference cost, there's usually one place that limits everything else. Working there tends to pay off even if you can't measure it cleanly at first. Working somewhere that isn't the bottleneck can look productive, with lots of experiments and lots of small gains, but it doesn't change the trajectory.

The second is to build my own reward signal. Public benchmarks are useful but they saturate, and people overfit to them. So I care a lot about evaluations that reflect what we actually want the model to do, and about small, fast experiments that predict what happens at larger scale. That's similar to quant, really: if you can't trust your backtest, you can't trust anything. A lot of the real work is making the measurement trustworthy.

The third is taste, which is harder to explain. Over time you develop a feeling for which ideas are simple and scalable, and which are clever but fragile. I've found that simple ideas that respect compute and scale usually win. If something needs a lot of special tricks to work, I become suspicious.

And finally, I accept that some bets just won't be clear in advance. In quant you diversify across strategies. In research you can do something similar: put most of your effort into directions you have strong conviction in, and keep a smaller portion for things that are uncertain but could be important. Then you stay honest with yourself and cut what isn't working, without getting too attached.

So the reward is less clear, but it isn't absent. You just have to put more work into seeing it.

fable-5.1.text:
In quant investing the feedback loop is brutally honest. You put a strategy on, and the market tells you within weeks whether you were right. Large models don't give you that. You can spend six months on a direction, burn through a huge amount of compute, and still not know whether it failed because the idea was wrong or because you didn't push it far enough.

So the first thing I changed was how I think about reward itself. In quant, reward is money, and it arrives on a fixed schedule. In model research, I had to stop waiting for an external number to validate the work and start building my own internal signals. Scaling curves are the closest thing we have. If something gets better in a clean, predictable way as you add data and compute, that's a kind of truth that doesn't depend on anyone's opinion. If the curve bends or stalls, that's also information, even if nobody is handing you a P&L statement for it.

The second thing is that I became much more willing to bet on things that look obvious in hindsight. In markets, if something is obvious, it's already priced in. In models, the obvious thing is often simply undone because it's expensive or tedious. Cleaning data properly, running the ablations everyone skips, actually checking what the model learned rather than what the benchmark says it learned. There's no competition arbitraging away the value of careful work, so careful work is where a lot of the reward hides.

And the third thing, honestly, is taste. When the reward is sparse you have to lean on judgment about what matters, and that judgment is mostly built by being wrong many times. I try to pursue directions where, if it works, it changes how we build the next model, not just the current score on one leaderboard. If a result only moves one number and teaches us nothing, it's probably not worth the months.

So the answer is a combination: trust the scaling signal, do the unglamorous work others skip, and ask whether the outcome would change what we do next. That's a weaker guarantee than a Sharpe ratio, but it's what you get when the thing you're building doesn't exist yet.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between an unclear reward and an unclear question. In quantitative investing, the feedback is relatively direct: you have a result that tells you whether a strategy worked. In large-model development, an experiment can improve a metric without necessarily telling you whether you’re moving toward something important.

So I would start by asking: what limitation are we trying to understand, and if we overcome it, what becomes possible? Then I’d look for the smallest experiment that can test that judgment. You need a longer-term conviction about the direction, but you also need short feedback cycles that can prove you wrong.

For me, a direction is worth pursuing when even a failed experiment can clarify something important. If every outcome can be interpreted as success, then we haven’t defined the question well enough.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficult part is that you have to make decisions before you have a reliable signal. In quantitative investing, you can at least evaluate a strategy against a relatively clear objective. With large models, a promising direction may take a long time to show its value, and an improvement on a benchmark may not mean you’ve solved the underlying problem.

So I would start with a concrete question: what limitation are we trying to overcome, and why do we believe this approach can overcome it? Then I’d look for a small experiment that could change our minds. If we can’t say what evidence would make us abandon an idea, we probably haven’t defined it clearly enough.

You still need conviction to pursue something uncertain. But for me, that conviction should come from an explanation you can test, and it should evolve as the evidence comes in.
